title: Resting variability improved mouse-to-human 50 Hz predictions in selected Allen excitatory slice connections
abstract: We tested whether resting response variability improves prediction of 50 Hz response change across two Allen cortical slice samples without fitting to the target species. We trained ridge models on 493 mouse excitatory connections from 276 inferred animals or 162 human excitatory connections from 43 inferred donors. Adding variability to cell, wiring and assay features reduced mouse-to-human donor-weighted squared error by 46.18% against the base model and 49.40% against the mouse-mean predictor. The 98.75% donor bootstrap intervals were 18.54 to 60.11% and 16.24 to 60.71%. The bootstrap resampled both source and target donors and refit the models. Reverse transfer improved against the base model, but its gain interval against the human-mean predictor included zero. A strict layer-2/3 excitatory-endpoint subset failed to beat the mean in the mouse-to-human direction and had only 11 source connections. Species and region are confounded. Shared response estimates, selected connections and inferred donor labels limit mechanism claims. Original code, aggregate evidence, a figure, source hashes and external retrieval steps support reproduction. External records are not bundled.
